summary: Equatorial Guinea lies on the west coast of Central Africa, made up of a mainland part and islands such as Bioko; it was a Spanish colony, is the only African country with Spanish as an official language, and its economy is highly dependent on oil.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1778 Portugal ceded its rights to Bioko and the mainland portion to Spain under the Treaty of El Pardo, and in the late 19th century Spanish Claretian missionaries evangelized on a large scale and dominated colonial education. After independence in 1968 the dictator Francisco Macías Nguema persecuted the church and in 1978 even banned Catholicism; religious freedom was restored only after Obiang's coup in 1979, and Pope John Paul II visited in 1982. Catholicism remains the faith of the vast majority.

ranking.name: Protestant Christianity
ranking.description: In the mid-19th century American Presbyterian missionaries preached on Corisco Island and in Río Muni on the mainland, while Bioko had Methodists from Britain and Sierra Leone. During the Spanish colonial period Catholicism enjoyed official support and Protestant development was limited, so today it is a smaller minority.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs and others
ranking.description: The Fang preserve the ancestor cult of "Byeri" and the Bwiti tradition, and the Bubi of Bioko also have traditional rites of worshipping spirits. These beliefs often coexist with Catholicism, and few people identify as following only a traditional religion.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought mainly in modern times by merchants and migrants from West Africa and Cameroon. After oil was discovered in the 1990s, the number of foreign workers rose, and the Muslim population grew with it, but native Muslims are very few.

religion.background: The indigenous peoples of Equatorial Guinea practiced ancestor and nature worship. The Portuguese discovered Bioko in the 15th century, it passed to Spain after 1778, and in the late 19th century Spanish Catholic missionaries and British and American Protestant missionaries arrived in turn, with Catholicism becoming the mainstream through the promotion of colonial education. After independence in 1968 the Macías regime suppressed religion, and religious freedom was restored when Obiang came to power in 1979. Today Catholicism remains the faith of the vast majority, interwoven with traditional customs.

language.official: Spanish, French and Portuguese are the official languages.

ranking.name: Fang
ranking.description: The Fang are the most populous ethnic group in Equatorial Guinea, making up the vast majority of Río Muni on the mainland, having migrated in from the north around the 18th–19th centuries. After independence both presidents, Macías and Obiang, have been Fang, and the Fang dominate politics and the military, so Fang is the country's main everyday language.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spain held this land from 1778 and colonized actively in the late 19th century until independence in 1968, making Equatorial Guinea the only African country with Spanish as an official language. Spanish is used in government, education and the media, but fewer people have it as a mother tongue. To strengthen ties with neighboring countries the government later also made French (1998) and Portuguese (2010) official languages.

language.history: The indigenous languages of Equatorial Guinea mostly belong to the Bantu group, including Fang on the mainland, Bubi on Bioko, and the Portuguese-based Creole (Fa d'Ambu) on the island of Annobón. In the colonial period the cocoa plantations of Bioko brought in large numbers of Nigerian and Sierra Leonean laborers, giving rise to an English-based "Pidgin English". Spanish became the administrative and educational language from the 19th century, was retained as an official language after independence, and French and Portuguese were added at the end of the 20th century.

ranking.name: Pepper soup
ranking.description: A spicy clear soup boiled from fish or meat such as goat with plenty of chili, local spices and vegetables; the soup is bright red with a strong flavor and is often drunk hot.
ranking.history: Pepper soup is very common in Nigeria and Cameroon, and the name comes from the English "pepper soup". In the colonial period the cocoa plantations of Bioko brought in large numbers of Nigerian laborers, and their Pidgin English and food came with them, so pepper soup became popular in Equatorial Guinea. It is often believed to drive away cold and cure illness, and it is a popular dish at bars and evening gatherings.

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Boiled cassava or plantain is pounded in a wooden mortar into a soft, elastic dough, and pinched by hand into small pieces to dip in various stews and soups.
ranking.history: Pounding starchy dough is an ancient food tradition of Central and West Africa, and after the Portuguese introduced cassava from the Americas in the 16th century it became an important ingredient. In Equatorial Guinea fufu is the everyday staple of the Fang and other peoples, usually eaten by pinching off a small piece by hand and dipping it in sauce, representing the local diet of root crops with stews.

ranking.name: Chicken in palm sauce (poulet à la moambe)
ranking.description: Chicken stewed in a palm fruit sauce with onion, tomato and chili, the sauce thick and orange-red, eaten with rice or cassava.
ranking.history: Chicken in palm sauce originates in the Congo Basin and is a dish widely found in Central Africa, regarded as the national dish by the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The oil palm is native to Central and West Africa, and palm fruit is an important local source of fat. The dish came to Equatorial Guinea with movement of people among Central African countries and often appears at family gatherings and festivals.

ranking.name: Bitterleaf stew (ndolé)
ranking.description: Washed, de-bittered bitterleaf is stewed with peanut paste, with shrimp, beef or smoked fish added; the flavor is slightly bitter with a rich nutty aroma, eaten with plantain or rice.
ranking.history: Ndolé originates with the Duala people of coastal Cameroon and is regarded as Cameroon's national dish. The Fang of Equatorial Guinea belong to the same people as the Fang of southern Cameroon, with close contact on both sides of the border, so this dish has also become a common dish in Equatorial Guinea. The bitterleaf must be washed several times to remove its bitterness, making it time-consuming to prepare, and it is often made at weekends or festivals.

ranking.name: Fried plantain (plátano frito)
ranking.description: Ripe plantains are sliced or cut into pieces and fried in oil; the outside is crisp and fragrant and the inside soft and sweet, often served as a side with stews and grilled fish, and also a common street snack.
ranking.history: Plantain has been grown in Central Africa for hundreds of years and is an important everyday source of starch for Equatorial Guineans. The name "plátano frito" is Spanish, reflecting the linguistic influence left by Spanish colonization. Fried plantain is simple to make, is often eaten with fish, chicken or beans, and is also a common snack sold by street vendors.
